evidence.snippet: Over the past 8 weeks we’ve gone from being comfortable with energy as being the primary driver of the pair ~> French fiscal concerns taking over --> US-led rate differentials driving EURUSD lower (Waller/CPI...) --> what we perceive to be significant macro-agnostic USD demand dictating the path. On France - keep half an eye on the rise of Lisnard into 2027, especially if you like to dream of a fatter RIGHT tale in Euro ... Sovereigns have turned better buyers of Dollars in Q4, US companies have been issuing in Euros and repatriating back into Dollars, and net M&A has turned LHS EURUSD. With discretionary macro names either being put in/electing to sit in the sin-bin, or perhaps just a function of being too busy fighting fires elsewhere - think equities, gold, crypto, EM - the impact of any macro-agnostic flow has become even more pronounced. As you get towards December some of these pressures should abate - the corporate issuance schedule starts to peter out. A critical 24hrs 9/10th Dec could support a lower Dollar as: 1) The FOMC deliver 25 BPS 2) They don’t pre-commit to a January hike 3) We potentially witness a negative MoM US CPI for Nov to somewhat dilute the last three beats. We estimate that the latest wave of macro-agnostic Dollar demand could have been worth up to ~150/200bps in EURUSD on the way down to the 1.0881 lows. We think the current intensity of supply is unlikely to remain a durable theme into year end -1.1010/25 is a hugely important pivot to watch over month end, and we would err on the side of ending the year closer to 1.12 than 1.0750 (ref 1.0975 spot). In cash we plan on buying a month end dip to 1.0930/40 OCO a breakup through 1.1010/25, overlaying perhaps with year-end -1.12 calls if you want to add some leverage.”

items.original_title: FinancialJuice: ING: The EUR

evidence.headline: FinancialJuice: ING: The EUR
evidence.snippet: It was confirmed yesterday that Pablo Hernández de Cos will become the next European Central Bank president. The announcement had little impact on the euro, having been widely expected for some time. De Cos is also unlikely to usher in any radical change at the ECB. While considered a dovish member during his time on the Governing Council, he is now seen primarily as a consensus builder. We doubt markets will draw strong monetary policy conclusions from his appointment for now, particularly as German economist Markus Brunnermeier, who leans hawkish, is reportedly leading the race for the Chief Economist role. The ongoing recovery in risk sentiment does not offer a clear directional signal for EUR/USD. Rebounding equities are being offset by a recovery in front-end USD swap rates, with the gap versus euro rates narrowing by around 6bp since yesterday. We think a 1.09-1.11 range can continue to dominate into December's central bank meetings. This morning brings November flash CPI estimates from France and Spain, ahead of Tuesday’s eurozone-wide release. October’s ECB minutes - published yesterday - confirmed a tightening bias, but policymakers remain uncertain about the dynamics in second-round inflation effects. For now, that should keep the ECB’s rhetoric broadly hawkish, with another hike likely in December. Beyond that, however, core inflation will need to accelerate to justify further tightening. S&P reviews France's rating today, which could slightly weigh on the euro late in the session.

items.original_title: FinancialJuice: Credit Ágricole: Eurozone Inflation

evidence.headline: FinancialJuice: Credit Ágricole: Eurozone Inflation
evidence.snippet: We expect Eurozone headline HICP to decrease in November, from 4.03% to 3.76% YoY  We expect the decline in Brent prices to drive down motor fuels in November. It would be partially offset by the ongoing transmission to consumer prices from recent months' surge in gas and electricity prices. We think energy HICP will recede from 21% to around 18% YoY. Likewise, we are tracking a marginal decline in food HICP, from 1.53% to 1.49% YoY, driven by some decline in fruit and vegetable prices as the aftermath of this summer's droughts fade. We anticipate an increase in core HICP for the third month in a row, from 2.56% to 2.61% YoY, led by a new rise in core goods HICP due to IT equipment. It would be partially offset by a slight decrease in services HICP, from 3.31% to 3.29% YoY, driven by a partial easing in tourism-related services after two consecutive strong prints. We have HICP ex-tobacco at 3.75% YoY, 4bp below the fixing as at Thursday 26 November. We have FR CPI ex-tobacco at 3.06% YoY, 13bp below the fixing. Still waiting for spillover effects from the energy crisis We continue to think the spillover effects from the current energy shock will continue to very gradually materialise later in Q4, but will bite essentially during H127. The recent relative drop in gas wholesale prices led us to slightly reduce our core inflation path. We now expect HICPx to reach 3.73% YoY in Dec-26, 3.12% in Jun-27 and 2.03% in Dec-27. Finally, we expect core HICP at 2.21% YoY in Dec-26, 3.00% in Jun-27 and 2.71% in Dec-27.
